questions.stem: A project costs 18 000 dollars now and returns 4000, 5000, 6000, 6000 and 7000 dollars at the ends of years 1 to 5 respectively. Its net present value at annual discount rate $r$ is defined by $NPV(r)=-18000+\sum_{t=1}^5 C_t/(1+r)^t$. The internal rate of return is the value of $r$ giving zero NPV.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the net present value at a 6% discount rate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the internal rate of return, as an annual percentage.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At a required return of 10%, decide whether the project has a positive NPV. Give one reason the calculation alone does not guarantee a profitable outcome.

steps.text: Discount every return for its own number of years and subtract the initial cost.
The internal rate is $15.245771\%$ per year.
$NPV(0.10)=2721.0138$ dollars, which is positive; the model meets the required return.
Future returns are forecasts; costs, timing or cash flows may differ, so a positive model NPV does not remove commercial risk.

questions.stem: The radius of a cylindrical tank is recorded as 2.40 m to the nearest 0.01 m. Its height is recorded as 5.2 m to the nearest 0.1 m. The nominal volume is calculated from these recorded values. Use the standard half-unit rounding intervals.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the largest possible percentage by which the nominal volume overstates the true volume. Use the true volume in the denominator.

steps.text: Volume $\pi r^2h$ increases with each positive dimension.
The nominal volume is $94.096983$ m$^3$; the overstatement is greatest at the lower true-volume bound.

questions.stem:
A monthly energy bill consists of a fixed charge of 8 dollars, plus 0.18 dollars per kWh for the first 120 kWh and 0.32 dollars per kWh above 120. Monthly use $X$ has the following distribution.

| $x$ / kWh | 50 | 100 | 150 | 200 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $P(X=x)$ | 0.1 | 0.3 | 0.4 | 0.2 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the bill for 150 kWh.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the expected monthly bill.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the bill at the expected use $E(X)$ and compare it with part (b). Explain the difference.

steps.text: Weight those four bills by their probabilities.
$E(X)=135$ kWh and its bill is $34.40$ dollars, below the expected bill.
The tariff is not one linear rule across the full range; high-use months incur the higher marginal rate, so substituting the mean use does not give the mean bill.

questions.stem:
A researcher records incident counts in 200 independent equal-duration intervals. The complete ungrouped counts sum to 400. Their grouped frequencies are

| Count | 0 | 1 | 2 | $\ge3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Observed | 20 | 58 | 62 | 60 |

Test the fit of a Poisson model at the 5% level, estimating its mean from these same observations.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the Poisson mean.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find all four expected frequencies.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State the degrees of freedom and find the test $p$-value.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State a conclusion in context.

steps.text: Use Poisson probabilities with the fitted mean 2; pool all counts at least 3 into the last cell.
$p=0.16524229>0.05$, so do not reject the Poisson model. This is insufficient evidence of lack of fit, not proof that the model is true.

questions.stem:
A crop response $Y$ is modelled by $Y=80-Ae^{-kt}$, with $A,k>0$ and $t$ in weeks. The value 80 is a proposed saturation level. Data are

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Y$ | 18.1 | 31.9 | 44.3 | 51.4 | 58.9 |

Fit by least squares to the transformed linear relationship.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State a linearized equation and find its fitted slope and intercept.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find $A$ and $k$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the fitted initial response and explain why the assumed saturation level cannot be established from these five early observations alone.

steps.text: The observations do not reach the long-run plateau. Other saturation levels/models may fit early data, so 80 remains a modelling assumption requiring later evidence.

questions.stem: Individual service times are independent, right-skewed, with population mean 18 minutes and standard deviation 12 minutes. For sample sizes greater than 30, use the central limit theorem to approximate the distribution of the sample mean.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For a sample of 64 customers, estimate the probability that their mean service time exceeds 20 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For samples of 64, find a bound exceeded by only 1% of sample means.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the smallest integer sample size greater than 30 for which the approximate probability of a sample mean above 20 is at most 0.025. Check the neighbouring sample size.

steps.text: The approximate sampling distribution is $\bar X\sim N(18,(12/8)^2)$.
The tails for $n=138$ and $n=139$ are $0.02512146$ and $0.024708796$ respectively, straddling 0.025.

parts.label: b

questions.stem: A contamination rate is suspected to exceed 0.02. In a design for a one-tailed exact binomial test, $n$ independent packets will be sampled and the null hypothesis will be rejected if at least two are contaminated. Choose the largest sample size whose Type I error probability is strictly below 0.05.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses for contamination probability $p$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the largest permitted value of $n$, checking the next integer.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: For this sample size, find the power of the test when the true contamination probability is 0.12.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why increasing the sample size without changing the rejection rule is not automatically permitted.

steps.text: The largest size is $n=18$, with Type I probability $0.049508833$.
With the threshold fixed at two, increasing n raises the null probability of rejection as well as power; a larger n can violate the Type I error limit.
